title: Excuses (Luke 14:15–24)
hookLine: a field, oxen, a marriage: good reasons to miss the feast

cards: Sorry, can't make it tonight, something's come up. Most of us have sent that message, and usually the reason is real enough: work ran late, the kids are tired, we need a night in.
Back at the same dinner table, a guest says something pious and safe: "Blessed is he that shall eat bread in the kingdom of God." A lovely thought about a feast someday.
Jesus answers with a story about a feast right now, and the very human art of the polite excuse.

teach.h: COME, FOR ALL THINGS ARE READY.
teach.b: A man prepares a great supper and invites many. In that world, guests were often invited ahead of time, then a servant came to fetch them when the meal was ready. That's this moment.
The servant goes out with the message, in the King James Bible: "Come; for all things are now ready." And then: "they all with one consent began to make excuse." All of them.
And they're good excuses. "I have bought a piece of ground, and I must needs go and see it: I pray thee have me excused." The second: "I have bought five yoke of oxen, and I go to prove them."
Ten oxen, a big purchase; he wants to test them. The third doesn't even ask to be excused: "I have married a wife, and therefore I cannot come." Land, business, family.
Not one of them is a bad thing.
Some commentators point out that nobody buys a field without seeing it, or oxen without trying them, so the excuses may be thinner than they sound.
Either way, the host is left with a feast and an empty hall. He's angry, and then he does something astonishing.

Go out quickly, he tells the servant, into the streets and lanes of the city, and bring in the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind. When there's still room, go further, to the highways and hedges.

teach.h: THEY ALL WITH ONE CONSENT BEGAN TO MAKE EXCUSE.
teach.b: The story isn't against fields, oxen or marriages. It's about good things becoming the reason we miss the best thing. And in the story the invitation never closes: the servant keeps going out until the house is full.

how: Many Christians hear this story as an invitation to worship and to the Lord's Supper, and some churches echo the servant's words when they invite people to the table at communion.

games.q: you're the host. the feast is ready and every guest has sent an excuse. what do you do?
o: cancel the feast and give the food away.
send out for the poor, the maimed, the halt and the blind, and keep going until the house is full.
eat alone, and never invite them again.
games.why: he sends into the streets and lanes, then the highways and hedges, "that my house may be filled."

practice: Think back over the last few weeks and what you said no to: a call from an old friend, a community event, a quiet time of prayer you kept postponing, a walk someone suggested.
Without judging yourself, notice which noes were honest rest and which were a field and five oxen. If you pray, listen for the words: come, for all is ready.

wordCard.voice: Excuses. A field, five yoke of oxen and a new marriage: good reasons, given all at once, to miss a feast that was already ready.

orig.note: Greek: to beg off, to make excuse. what all the guests did, with one consent.

carryVoice: Your line: come, for all is ready. Honest rest isn't an excuse. Day five hundred fifty-five, done.
